3.text: may be calves; but they must be tame, fit for harness, in a word, “lustful

4.text: calves” (g̣iˊʟi-qäiˊut). — that is, lustful for urine. The domestication of rein-

5.text: deer among the Chukchee is notoriously based on the reindeer’s fondness for

6.text: urine.¹ Besides reindeer, the bride and groom take with them meat-puddings,

7.text: a favorite delicacy of the Chukchee.² The number of these puddings varies

8.text: generally according to the number of the reindeer, although two and three

9.text: times that number are sometimes taken. According to Chukchee ideas of

10.text: the family and family-group, the groom has to be assisted by his nearest

11.text: kinsmen; but this assistance is left to their individual free-will. Generally,

12.text: however, one or two of the blood relatives in the male line (kɪrñeˊ-tuˊmg̣ɪt,

13.text: “male-buck companions”), or of relatives by marriage (takaˊlhɪt, “husbands of

14.text: wife-sisters”³), contribute each a reindeer or two. To receive assistance from

15.text: more than two men is not customary. The other reindeer are given by the

16.text: groom himself. With the reindeer, the relatives send an equal number of

17.text: puddings, and sometimes two and three times the number. These puddings

18.text: have a symbolic significance. If a relative, for instance, intends to contribute

19.text: a reindeer or two, but at the time is not able to do it, he sends only the

20.text: puddings, thereby assuming the obligation to furnish the reindeer to the bride’s

21.text: father. Thus, instead of reindeer, puddings alone are sometimes sent to the

22.text: bride’s home. Along with the puddings, other delicacies of the Chukchee

23.text: bill of fare are brought down: such as marrow, extracted from the tubular bones

24.text: of the leg, and frozen, of which up to ten pounds is sometimes brought; rein-

25.text: deer-brains, also frozen; tongues; fat morsels of meat. On their arrival at

26.text: the bride’s camp, the bride and groom are again anointed, the bride’s family

27.text: mark is painted on their faces, and the bride makes a sacrifice to the hearth

28.text: of her home. A feast follows, at which all the provisions brought for the

29.text: occasion are consumed. On the following day the couple return home, where

30.text: the rite of anointment is once more repeated, and the husband’s family mark

31.text: is painted on their faces. Having thus taken leave of her family hearth

32.text: and its marks of anointing, the bride finally links herself to her new hearth,

33.text: and becomes a member of a new family.

34.text: Marriage-Ruptures. — Notwithstanding the accompanying sacrifice, Chuk-

35.text: chee marriages are not at all permanent. On the contrary, the anointment

36.text: with blood, and other rites, are obviously intended to strengthen marriage-ties,

37.text: but fail to attain that end. These rites foreshadow the religious sanction of

38.text: marriage, which in other cultures develops so powerfully. Among the Chuk-

39.text: chee the marriage-tie is broken very easily, and for a variety of reasons,

40.text: advanced by either the wife’s or the husband’s family. If the father or

41.text: mother of the groom is not satisfied with the bride, they have the right to
